title: The wandering teacher
hook: Patrul Rinpoche, who wandered as a beggar and taught anyone

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Karmapas, a teacher recognized life after life, with a crown and a monastery waiting. Today, a teacher who wanted none of that.

Tibetans tell a story about a traveling lama with a large party and a lot of baggage. On the road he meets a scruffy old man in a worn sheepskin coat and puts him to work: fetch the water, boil the tea, carry the bags. The old man does it all, cheerfully. Days later, at a great gathering, the lama walks in to hear the teacher everyone has come for, and the one on the high seat is the old man in the sheepskin coat. The lama, the story says, wanted the ground to swallow him. Today, Patrul Rinpoche.
screen: `A LAMA WITH A LOT OF BAGGAGE.` → `AN OLD MAN BOILS THE TEA.` → `THE OLD MAN ON THE HIGH SEAT.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. The old man in those stories is Patrul Rinpoche, a Tibetan teacher remembered across the Nyingma school and beyond. He was recognized as a tulku, like yesterday's Karmapas, and could have lived surrounded by honor. Instead he spent much of his life wandering, often alone, dressed like a beggar, sleeping in caves and in the open. Second, what he taught, and to whom. He taught anyone who asked: monks, nomads, children. Tradition remembers him teaching Shantideva's Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life over and over, so that ordinary people knew it well. And he wrote Words of My Perfect Teacher, a book on the foundations of practice, full of plain speech and sharp humor, which Tibetan students still read. Third, how he treated gifts. The stories say that when people offered him silver or fine things, he left them lying where they were, or gave them away, and moved on with almost nothing. The point is not that gifts are bad, or that the givers were wrong to give. He had nothing to guard, so nothing could hold him in one place. Fourth, why beggar teacher fits. For Patrul, humility wasn't a pose. It was a way of keeping the teaching free of the teacher. If nobody bows to the coat, then people have to listen to the words.
screen: `A TULKU WHO CHOSE THE ROAD.` · `HE TAUGHT ANYONE WHO ASKED.` · `GIFTS LEFT WHERE THEY LAY.` · `NOTHING BEING GUARDED.` · then, large: `THE BEGGAR TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a moment when you wanted credit, a job done well, a kindness nobody noticed, and feel how much you wanted to be seen, without judging it. Then, on the out-breath, set the credit down, the way Patrul left gifts where they lay.
Patrul Rinpoche. The Nyingma tulku who chose the road, dressed like a beggar, and taught anyone who asked. Today's word.
Your line: the beggar teacher. Nothing to guard, so nothing to hold him. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist students, especially in the Nyingma school, read Patrul Rinpoche's Words of My Perfect Teacher as a guide to the preliminary practices, and stories of his humility are retold by teachers as examples.

chat.says: Why would a respected teacher dress like a beggar on purpose?
options: Humility kept the teaching free of him: people listened to words, not the coat.
Because accepting any gift is wrong, and good teachers own nothing.
He lost his monastery and had no choice but to wander the roads.
chat.meaning: Patrul could have lived in honor as a tulku. He chose the road, so people had to listen to the teaching instead of bowing to the coat.
